slides.heading: Class Photos
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Greedy Algorithms
slides.narration: Let's solve Class Photos, an easy greedy algorithms problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Equal numbers of red and blue shirted students; all of one colour in the back row, each back-row student strictly taller than the person in front.
Is a photo possible?
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Equal numbers of red and blue shirted students; all of one colour in the back row, each back-row student strictly taller than the person in front. Is a photo possible?

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Sort both groups.
The taller group must stand in the back, and then every back student must be taller than the one in front.
slides.narration: Sort both groups. The taller group must stand in the back, and then every back student must be taller than the one in front.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: try every arrangement → factorial time
Optimal: sort both, compare pairwise → O(n log n)
Pairing sorted with sorted is the best possible matching
slides.narration: Trying every arrangement would be factorial. If any arrangement works, pairing the sorted groups position by position works too, so we sort and compare, in n log n.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Sort red and blue shirts
2. The group with the taller tallest goes in the back
3. Check every pair strictly
4. Any failure means false
slides.narration: Step by step. First, sort red and blue shirts. Second, the group with the taller tallest goes in the back. Third, check every pair strictly. Fourth, any failure means false.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Sort both groups; tallest blue 9 > tallest red 8
slides.narration: Sort both groups by height. The tallest blue student, nine, beats the tallest red, eight, so blue must be the back row.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.narration: Position 0: back 9 versus front 8. The back student is strictly taller, so this pair works.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.narration: Position 2: back 5 versus front 4. The back student is strictly taller, so this pair works.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.narration: Position 4: back 2 versus front 1. The back student is strictly taller, so this pair works.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We sort both lists in descending order, choose the back row by comparing the first elements, then check every position strictly. Any failure returns false.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(n log n)
Space: O(1)
slides.narration: Time is O of n log n. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Strictly taller required: equal heights fail
Decide back row from the tallest of each group
Groups have equal size
slides.narration: Heights must be strictly greater, so equal heights fail. Decide which colour goes in the back from the tallest students, then never switch.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Explain why sorted pairing is optimal (exchange argument)
Follow-up: count arrangements, or allow mixed rows
slides.narration: Justify the greedy with an exchange argument: swapping any pair out of sorted order can't help.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Sort both groups.
Complexity: O(n log n)
slides.narration: To recap Class Photos: Sort both groups. The taller group must stand in the back, and then every back student must be taller than the one in front. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
